I'm not too familiar with the Category Theory part of the codebase. Does anyone know if we heve the tools to define a functor F on the category of finite dimensional Vector Spaces which induces a smooth map Hom(V,W) → Hom(F(V),F(W))for any vector spaces V and W? Also, the continuous analogue? It would be very useful for defining tensors on manifolds!

See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_functor
What's the codomain of F? Ah, fin-dim vector spaces again.
Yes, F takes the category "Finite Dimensional Vector Spaces" to itself. I'm not really sure what is the best way to express this in Lean

This is only about vector spaces over the reals or some kind of complete normed field, right?

Can you give an example of a non-smooth functor?
Yes, the field should be equipped with some "smoothness", so Reals or Complex. The idea is that for every vector space X, the functor induces a map F : GL(X) -> GL(X) which we require to be smooth.

I can give a counter-example where it fails, but it requires axiom of choice: We can take a wild field automorphism ϕ : ℂ -> ℂ, then we can apply ϕ entrywise to elements of GL(n, ℂ) -> GL(n, ℂ). And the fact that ϕ is an automorphism ensures this is functorial--but ϕ is not smooth, it is discontinuous.

Actually, for a better example, we can take ϕ(z) = z* to simply be the complex conjugate, which is not ℂ-differentiable (it is continuous but not holomorphic). So this gives an example of a continuous functor which is not a smooth functor. I think in the real case however, it is always smooth.

Thanks for illuminating example: on objects it is V↦V⊗C,ϕC.V\mapsto V\otimes_{\mathbb{C},\phi}\mathbb{C}.V↦V⊗C,ϕ​C. Yes I can imagine that this is one of those situations where all constructive functors are smooth. We definitely have the tools to construct what you want, you just put a norm on the hom sets (we will already have the vector space structure I should think) and then add the condition that the map is smooth. This is a very elegant predicate -- have the community thought about it already? @Yury G. Kudryashov ?

In algebraic geometry a different approach is used and we have lots more machinery for that. Instead of considering vector spaces over C you consider free modules over C-algebras and demand that your functor makes sense on these. The gluing process then takes you from affine schemes to schemes. The C-algebra in question here would be the C^infty functions on an open set in the manifold and there is a hugely general concept of a grothendieck topology on a category which generalises all of this out of the park.

Yes, I imagine this can be generalized very heavily. I was hoping there might be some highly general implementation in Mathlib and I can just import it into my manifolds code. The main application in differential geometry is simply the fact that smooth functors naturally induce operations on smooth vector bundles. And that natural isomorphisms of functors correspond to vector bundle isomorphisms.
Somebody needs to write that highly general implementation :-)

Mathlib knows that units of a normed algebra are a manifold. I suspect the step "put some norm on your vector spaces, then Hom(V,W)Hom(V, W)Hom(V,W) is a normed space and thus a manifold" being non-canonical is one reason it is not in mathlib. (Aside from the fact that nobody needed it yet.)
I would imagine that there is an intrinsic notion of a function being smooth or more generally C^n between two finite-dimensional real vector spaces. Do we have this?

Or am I wrong here? The theorem I learnt was that all norms on a fdvs/\R are equivalent so induce the same topology, so there's an intrinsic notion of continuous. Does the argument generalise?

The docs#ModuleTopology in mathlib is this intrinsic topology btw
I would imagine so also (and didn't think about it for more than one minute yet). I don't think mathlib has such a notation so far; we didn't need it (yet?).

An ordinary category is like a category that is enriched over the category of types. It seems you are considering categories that are enriched over a suitable category of manifolds. Then, smooth functors should be enriched functors between two such enriched categories docs#CategoryTheory.EnrichedFunctor

I do not think there is an intrinsic notion of smoothness. There are exotic smooth structures on R^4 which are homeomorphic to the standard R^4, so they respect the induced module topology, but they are not diffeomorphic. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_R4
But I bet they don't come from norms? Or am I wrong?
Yes, I see what you mean, the Frechet derivative only requires a norm so it should be uniquely determined by the NormedSpace. I think this is precisely how Mathlib defines Fderiv on a CompleteSpace.

The exotic R^4 structures are not really compatible with the vector space structure at all. If we require any sort of compatibility (e.g. a Lie Group) then the smooth structure should be uniquely determined.

Joël Riou said:

An ordinary category is like a category that is enriched over the category of types. It seems you are considering categories that are enriched over a suitable category of manifolds. Then, smooth functors should be enriched functors between two such enriched categories docs#CategoryTheory.EnrichedFunctor

Just to clarify "suitable category of manifolds"-- Do you mean should consider the monoidal category "objects = smooth manifolds" and "morphisms = smooth maps"? And then consider the enriched category over that?

I think that this question about exotic smooth structures might be a red herring. My guess (although I might be wrong) is that you are only interested in Euclidean norms on a finite-dimensional vector space coming from a choice of basis, and the dfifferent choices of bases are all related via formulae using only matrix multiplication and inverse, which are certainly smooth. So it seems to me that there is a canonical CωC^\omegaCω real manifold structure on a real vector space (e.g. Hom(V,W)Hom(V,W)Hom(V,W)) and you need some version of that. What I am a bit confused by (and this is due to my lack of familiarity with the manifold side of mathlib) is that I was taught that "nnn-dimensional manifold" made sense and this is "manifold modelled on Rn\R^nRn) but we seem to have a more general concept in mathlib, where you're modelled on a model space. I was talking about change of model space in the Riemann surfaces thread. I think I don't even understand how to say "let XXX be an nnn-dimensional manifold" in Lean in some sense, I have to choose which Rn\R^nRn I'm talking about.

Re enriched categories: the first thing to do is to enrich the category of finite-dimensional real vector spaces using docs#CategoryTheory.EnrichedCategory .

I think that this would be an interesting exercise because I am confused about what the category of manifolds will look like when you're trying to keep track of model spaces as well.

Correct, in practice I am only interested in Euclidean norms on a finite-dimensional vector space. This is exactly what ModelWithCornersSelf 𝕜 E = 𝓘(𝕜, E) is supposed to give you, since it relies only on E being a NormedSpace over 𝕜. This is the "canonical Rn\R^nRn" I think you're talking about.

As for change of model space, you're free to choose any model I as long as the underlying field 𝕜 remains fixed. All smoothness definitions like MFDeriv are written for manifolds of different models but fixed 𝕜 (for example, a smooth map between a real manifold without boundary and a real manifold with boundary makes sense. But a smooth map between a real manifold and a complex manifold doesn't.) So I think the relevant monoidal category here is the "category of 𝕜-manifolds".

I am going to try to implement this today and see how far I can get
I see we do have bundled morphisms so that's your category structure, so perhaps the first challenge is making k-manifolds into a monoidal category
Working on it now. I'm going to track my progress on #PR reviews > #38223 The Category of C^n Manifolds

Kevin Buzzard said:

I would imagine that there is an intrinsic notion of a function being smooth or more generally C^n between two finite-dimensional real vector spaces. Do we have this?

This may be a bit tangent to the topic of this thread, but there is - just like how you can equip any module over a topological ring with docs#moduleTopology and get the standard topology in the case of finite-dimensional vector spaces over R, you can equip any module over a diffeological ring with the finest diffeology making it into a diffeological module and get the standard diffeology in the case of finite-dimensional vector spaces over R or C (see e.g. here). We do not have this in mathlib though because I haven't yet PR'd enough diffeology, and we couldn't have it as an instance for the same reason docs#moduleTopology is not an instance - it would conflict with the standard diffeology in the case of infinite-dimensional normed spaces.

With our current definition of diffeological spaces this would only work for smooth maps by the way because diffeological spaces are only defined for smoothness degree ∞\infty∞ and over R\mathbb RR in the literature, but both the definition and the argument generalise to arbitrary smoothness degrees and normed ground fields - I still think that having API for such generalised diffeological spaces in mathlib would be worthwhile, and even suggested it as a topic for my master thesis to my advisors, but we eventually converged on a different topic so it is unfortunately not very high on my list of priorities now.
Aah but docs#IsModuleTopology is an instance and I've found it very useful. Is there an analogous class here?

yep, IsFineDiffeology - but again, not yet upstreamed. It works completely analogously to docs#IsModuleTopology because in both cases it really is just built on top of categorical structure that the two categories share
